source: Liao & Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining
finding: CompressARC trains a tiny net from random init on one puzzle only, minimising description length (reconstruction plus KL). It solves 20% of ARC-AGI-1 public eval puzzles.
numbers: 76K parameters. 2000 steps, about 20 min per puzzle on one RTX 4070. Pass@2: 20% eval (400 puzzles), 34.75% train (400). No pretraining, no ARC training set.
quote: CompressARC ... solves 20% of evaluation puzzles by minimizing the description length (MDL) of the target puzzle purely during inference time.
limits: Public eval, not the private set. Score is pass@2. Single paper from the authors.
agent_relevance: Shows an alternative solver that needs no pretrained model and no data beyond the task. Candidate fallback for grid puzzles.

source: Liao & Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining
finding: Accuracy rises smoothly with inference-time steps and with number of allowed guesses.
numbers: Eval pass@2 by step: 100 steps 1.25%, 300 steps 10.75%, 500 steps 15.0%, 1000 steps 19.25%, 2000 steps 20.0%. At 2000 steps eval pass@1 18.5%, pass@10 26.0%, pass@100 31.25%, pass@1000 33.75%.
limits: Gains flatten after about 1000 steps. The gap between pass@2 and pass@1000 shows the right answer is often sampled but not picked.
agent_relevance: Compute-accuracy curve is the budget lever. Better answer selection could add up to 13 points on eval at no extra training.

source: Liao & Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining
finding: The train set is easier: the same method scores higher at every budget.
numbers: Train set pass@1 30.25%, pass@2 34.75%, pass@1000 52.75% at 2000 steps (130 h for 400 puzzles). Eval takes 138 h.
limits: Compute is serial, one puzzle at a time.
agent_relevance: Expect a 14-point drop from an easy to a hard puzzle set. Do not trust train-set numbers.

source: Liao & Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining
finding: Authors list what the model can and cannot do. Failures follow the architecture: no long range, no counting, no topology.
numbers: Can: infilling, cropping, connecting dots with lines (incl 45 degrees), same-colour detection, adjacency, short translations. Cannot: counting, rotation, reflection, rescaling, duplication, connectivity, planning, long-range pattern extension, repeating an operation many times.
limits: Abilities were built into layers by hand. Authors say they are endowed by select layers. Not general MDL magic.
agent_relevance: MDL picks the shortest rule only inside the language the net can express. Treat it as a solver for local, colour-mapping puzzles only.

source: Liao & Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining
finding: A plain U-Net trained under the same target-puzzle-only terms does far worse, so the MDL objective and architecture matter, not per-puzzle training alone.
numbers: U-Net baseline row in Table 1 reads 0.75% on public eval (table columns garbled in text extraction, so approximate). Puzzles with shape change skipped. U-Net with augmentation was worse on train: 2.5% without, 1% with.
limits: Table text garbled in my extraction. Baseline is the authors own, and works only on same-shape puzzles.
agent_relevance: Per-puzzle training alone is not the active ingredient. The compression pressure is.

source: Liao & Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining
finding: Design experiments that failed: a hierarchical VAE collapsed, convolution layers amplified noise, a KL floor never rescued a collapsed tensor.
numbers: Hierarchical decoder: first layer took all the KL, later layers useless, so one layer kept. Tropical convolution worked on toy puzzles but not ARC train. KL floor: authors never saw a collapsed tensor recover.
limits: No ablation table with numbers. Runs vary: sometimes a needed latent collapsed to zero KL and the puzzle failed.
agent_relevance: Run-to-run variance is real. Budget for restarts with a new seed.

source: Liao & Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining
finding: Answer extraction needs denoising. Sampled grids have random wrong pixels, so the authors vote over training steps with an exponential moving average and weight by uncertainty.
numbers: EMA decay 0.97. Answers before step 150 dropped (weight e^-10). EMA answers weight e^-4. Further weight e^(-10 x uncertainty).
limits: Hand-tuned rules, not ablated with numbers.
agent_relevance: Voting over a trajectory with an uncertainty weight is the same trick LLM agents use for self-consistency.

source: Liao & Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining
finding: Reference points: average human solves 76.2% of ARC train tasks, experts 98.5%. CompressARC train 34.75% is under half of average human.
numbers: Human 76.2% (average), 98.5% (expert), from LeGris et al 2024 as cited. CompressARC train 34.75%.
limits: Human number is for the train set, not eval.
agent_relevance: The alternative solver is far from human level. Use it as a supplement, not a replacement.

source: Liao & Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining
finding: Authors name untried improvements: shared puzzle embedding or hypernetwork, copy-shape layers, regularising the weights. The weights are not counted in the code length.
numbers: Authors call not compressing the weights reckless because they contribute many bits.
limits: So this is partial MDL: only the latent code and decoder fit are scored.
agent_relevance: Do not claim a principled Occam guarantee. The compression is only a training pressure.

source: ARC Prize Foundation (2025) ARC Prize 2025 results and analysis
finding: On the harder ARC-AGI-2 private set CompressARC scores about 4%. It won 3rd place in the paper awards, behind TRM (about 8%).
numbers: CompressARC paper award 3rd ($5k), about 4% on ARC-AGI-2, 20-34% on ARC-AGI-1. TRM 1st paper award, 7M parameters, about 45% ARC-AGI-1 and 8% ARC-AGI-2. Kaggle ARC-AGI-2: NVARC 24.03%, ARChitects 16.53%, MindsAI 12.64%.
limits: Read through a summariser tool, not raw HTML. MindsAI score appears twice (12.64% and 15.42%). The 4% comes from an interview summary.
agent_relevance: Pure inference-time compression does not scale to harder puzzles. Do not expect it to carry hard items.

source: ARC Prize Foundation (2025) The Hidden Drivers of HRM Performance (ARC Prize analysis)
finding: Independent test of HRM: most gain comes from the outer refinement loop and from training on the eval tasks, not the hierarchy. This makes HRM close to test-time training.
numbers: ARC-AGI-1 semi-private (100 tasks) 32%, public eval claimed 41%. ARC-AGI-2 semi-private (120 tasks) 2%. Same-size transformer within about 5 points. 1 to 2 refinement loops adds 13 points. Training on only the 400 eval tasks gave 31% vs 41%. Per-task-only training estimated about 21%.
limits: Read through a summariser. The 21% is the authors guess, not a measured run.
agent_relevance: Claimed scores can drop on held-out sets. The per-task guess of 21% sits near CompressARC 20%.

source: Akyurek et al (2024) The Surprising Effectiveness of Test-Time Training for Few-Shot Learning
finding: Per-task fine-tuning at inference (LoRA) on augmented demonstrations lifts an LLM sharply on ARC. This is the main rival: it learns per puzzle but starts from a pretrained model.
numbers: TTT improves the fine-tuned model about 6x (5% to 29%) on an 80-task subset. 8B model: 53.0% on public validation; 61.9% ensembled with a program synthesizer. Ablations: no augmentations -16 tasks (55%), direct I/O format -11 tasks (38%), shared single adapter -7 tasks (24%), demo-output loss 26% to 29%. 1B and 3B equal after TTT.
limits: Needs a fine-tuned pretrained base. Validation split. The 80-task subset is small.
agent_relevance: Per-puzzle learning works much better with a prior (53% vs CompressARC 20%). The prior is worth about 30 points.

source: Li et al (2024) Combining Induction and Transduction for Abstract Reasoning
finding: Program writing (induction) and direct output prediction (transduction) solve different ARC tasks, stably across seeds. Ensembling helps a lot.
numbers: Transduction no TTT 37.50%; with TTT 43.25%; induction 10k samples 19.25%; ensemble 56.75% validation (two tries); with Akyurek TTT 61.9%. Average human 60.2%, best humans 98%.
limits: Needs synthetic training data of ARC programs. Validation split.
agent_relevance: CompressARC is a third family. Complementary solvers beat one solver, so test whether compression solves tasks the others miss.

source: Macfarlane & Bonnet (2024) Searching Latent Program Spaces
finding: A model that searches a latent program space by gradient at test time. Gradient search beats sampling and random starting points.
numbers: ARC eval ablation: encoder init + gradient search 9.1/13.25/15.0/15.5/15.5% across budgets; encoder sampling about 10.5%; Gaussian init + gradient 1.4% to 10.75%. Pattern task: training aware of test-time gradient 99.5% vs 67.5% without.
limits: Trained on re-ARC style data; ARC eval numbers low (about 15%). Different method, same spirit.
agent_relevance: Test-time search needs a good starting point from a learned prior. Scaffold analog: start from a proposed answer and refine.

source: Franzen, Disselhoff, Hartmann (2025) Product of Experts with LLMs: Boosting Performance on ARC
finding: Scoring candidate answers by likelihood under many views (augmentations) picks the right one more often. This is a code-length style selection used with test-time training.
numbers: 8B model: baseline 18.3%, +TTT 44.5%, +16 augmented samples 62.5%, +product of experts 67.6%. 3B: 14.9, 40.9, 52.9, 59.5. Full system 71.6% (286.5 of 400) on public eval at about 2 cents per task. TTT about 51 s per task on RTX 4090. ConceptARC 73.3%.
limits: Public eval, 2 guesses. Needs a fine-tuned 8B model.
agent_relevance: Selecting by summed negative log probability across views gave +5 to +7 points. Idea for our scaffold: re-score candidate answers under rephrasings.

source: Deletang et al (2024) Language Modeling Is Compression
finding: A big language model is a strong general compressor, beating PNG and FLAC on image and audio it was not trained on.
numbers: Chinchilla 70B compresses ImageNet patches to 43.4% of raw size (PNG 58.5%) and LibriSpeech to 16.4% (FLAC 30.3%).
limits: Needs a huge pretrained model; weights are not counted in the size.
agent_relevance: Prediction and compression are the same thing, so a prior-heavy LLM is already a compressor. CompressARC is the opposite pole: no prior, only per-task fit.

source: Huang et al (2024) Compression Represents Intelligence Linearly
finding: Across 31 public LLMs and 12 benchmarks, compression of external text tracks benchmark score almost linearly.
numbers: Pearson correlation about -0.95 per domain (knowledge, coding, math), about -0.93 on average.
limits: Correlation across models, not a test of per-task compression. Fine-tuned models are no longer general compressors.
agent_relevance: Supports code length as a quality signal across pretrained models, not inside one inference run.

source: Xu & Miikkulainen (2025) Neural Cellular Automata for ARC-AGI
finding: Per-task training without an MDL term (NCA) solves few tasks and mostly overfits. Contrast with CompressARC.
numbers: Of 400 train tasks, 172 feasible; NCA solved 23 perfectly (13.37% of feasible). About 10,000 parameters, 800 epochs, minutes per task. Largest failure group: fits training pairs but fails on new inputs.
limits: Excludes 228 tasks by grid-size and colour rules, so not comparable to CompressARC full sets. Cites CompressARC only in related work.
agent_relevance: Per-puzzle fits without pressure for short descriptions memorise. Compression is the regulariser that matters.

source: Chollet et al (2025) ARC-AGI-2: A New Challenge for Frontier AI Reasoning Systems
finding: On ARC-AGI-2, strong test-time-adaptation systems score low, while every task was solved by at least two non-expert humans.
numbers: ARC-AGI-2 semi-private vs ARC-AGI-1: o3 medium 3.0% vs 53.0%, ARChitects 2.5% vs 56.0%, o3-mini high 3.0% vs 34.5%, Claude 3.7 8K 0.9% vs 21.2%. Human average 2.7 minutes per task. o3 preview ARC-AGI-1: 76% low compute (about $200/task), 88% high (about $20,000/task).
limits: Snapshot of early 2025. Later systems did better.
agent_relevance: Methods tuned on ARC-AGI-1 collapse on v2. Expect compression solvers near the floor on hard novel items.

source: Liao & Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining
finding: Compute is the main boundary. 20 min a puzzle on a consumer GPU is far over what an interactive agent step can spend.
numbers: 138 h for 400 eval puzzles on one RTX 4070. Competition limit is 12 h per submission for the whole hidden set.
limits: Authors run one puzzle at a time and note parallel runs were not tried.
agent_relevance: Use only as a slow background solver for a few flagged items.

source: Liao (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (author blog)
finding: Blog restates the result and recipe and reports no quantitative ablation.
numbers: Adam, lr 0.01, betas 0.5 and 0.9, 2000 iterations, reconstruction error weighted 10x against KL. About 20 min per puzzle on RTX 4070.
limits: Read through a summariser. Same author as the paper; no outside replication found.
agent_relevance: The recipe is small enough to re-run. Worth testing on our ARC items as an honest control.

source: arXiv full-text search for CompressARC (run 2026-11-09)
finding: The search returns only the original paper. I found no independent replication or failed replication.
numbers: 1 search result. Semantic Scholar listed 4 citing items (a survey, an agentic frameworks study, NCA for ARC, a diffusion paper). I read the NCA and agentic study and found only passing mentions.
limits: Semantic Scholar returned 429, OpenAlex budget was gone, WebSearch budget was used up. Absence of replications is not proven.
agent_relevance: Treat the 20% figure as single-source until someone re-runs it.

source: Rasheed et al (2026) Agentic Frameworks for Reasoning Tasks: An Empirical Study
finding: Cites CompressARC but evaluates 22 agent frameworks on BBH, GSM8K and ARC. It does not test compression at inference time.
numbers: 19 of 22 frameworks completed all three benchmarks. 12 were consistent: mean accuracy 74.6-75.9%, 4-6 s per task, cost $0.14-0.18 per task.
limits: Not about MDL. Recorded only to show no LLM-agent study tests this idea.
agent_relevance: No LLM-agent evidence yet for compression as inference. Open gap.

source: Franzen, Disselhoff, Hartmann (2025) Product of Experts with LLMs: Boosting Performance on ARC
finding: The same likelihood-product selection transfers to Sudoku with no test-time training, and the authors give a result that the product beats a single random view in expectation.
numbers: Sudoku 3M dataset: product of experts raised top-1 accuracy to 53%, above picking the highest-probability sampled solution. Generation accuracy matched PoE accuracy, so if a correct solution is sampled it is consistently selected.
limits: Sudoku has fixed rules, so no TTT was used. Single-team result.
agent_relevance: Selection is the cheap part: when the right answer is in the candidate set, multi-view scoring finds it.

source: Akyurek et al (2024) The Surprising Effectiveness of Test-Time Training for Few-Shot Learning
finding: TTT also helps on BBH, not only ARC, and hierarchical voting over transformed inferences nearly reaches the oracle.
numbers: Compared with ARC, BBH has few demonstrations per task, so gains are smaller. Hierarchical voting beat flat voting and approached the oracle that picks the correct answer when present. Rotate/transpose/flip each help modestly alone; transpose worst.
limits: Exact BBH figures not recorded here. Per-task LoRA cost not compared with CompressARC.
agent_relevance: Voting over transformed views plus per-task adaptation is the working recipe; compression-only is weaker.
